utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me start off by staying that this marathon testimony that we have been hearing for two days now is the best confirmation of my warning to the public about the main tactical movement on the part of the Prosecution as regards the reversal of thesis or turning things upside down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Question for the witness. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't you worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, what Council for Human Rights are we talking about? Whose council is it? Whose Council for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Council for Human Rights and Freedoms was set up in the 1990s with the purpose of investigating the violence and terror perpetrated by Serb police and army against the Albanian population. It also investigated violence in general. It was an association of a humanitarian character. I think that you must know that this council was registered then at the Yugoslav Federation and it had its own seal, which I think was issued by Mr. Kambovski. I don't very well remember what office he had then, but this council operated in a public manner in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who founded it?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Council for Human Rights and Freedoms emerged as a necessity of the time. It was necessary to set it up as a result of violence and reprisals that follow the deprivation of autonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, can I ask you to listen to the question and try and deal with that. The question was: Who set it up?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was founded by a group of intellectuals, but there were others also who were honourable members of this council, but they were not Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And which intellectuals were these? A group of intellectuals. You and how many others?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not me who formed this council in Prishtina. The Council for Human Rights and Freedoms in Prishtina, it is a public fact when it was known -- it was transparent in the public currents, not only in Kosova, but also broad Kosova, I mean even beyond Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was founded by a group of Albanian intellectuals as their own organ; is that right? That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I said that in addition to Albanians, there were others who were members of this council but who were not Albanians. Of course, the initiative came from Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you say what you heard allegedly as the result of the work of your council; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We carried out the duties of the Council of Human Rights and Freedoms. We investigated cases of violence and reprisals committed by your police against the Albanian population of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I think enough has been said about that. You said, when you started your testimony, that you were dissatisfied. You spoke about your dissatisfaction with the Encyclopedia of Yugoslavia. Do you know that that encyclopedia was published by the lexicographical institute in Zagreb, in fact?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry that at your insistence I was -- I mean, I was not allowed to talk here about this encyclopedia of 1938. You said I am not an expert on that, but I want to inform this Honourable Chamber that I read this memorandum and that we paid with our own blood, all of us, in Kosova. This memorandum drafted by Cubrilovic. It was a very highly chauvinistic one. And the Academy of Sciences and Arts, after the war, operated precisely having this notorious memorandum of 1938 as its basis. I would like to remind you all here that even prior --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's enough, Mr. Kadriu. We must get through the evidence. Now, the next question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that from Kosovo and Metohija, the president of the encyclopedic committee was your own man of letters, Esad Mekuli?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The encyclopedia created discontent among the students and intellectuals of Albania then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question was, insofar as this is relevant, that Esad Mekuli was described as the president, I think, of the encyclopedia committee. Now, do you know if that is right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that. I only know that it gave rise to discontent because the Albanian population of Kosova were not given a deserved place in this encyclopedia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know who Esad Mekuli is?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, I knew who he was, because he had published collections of poems, and I used to read them. And I was educated in the humanitarian spirit that he preached through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. He was the president of the encyclopedic committee for Kosovo and Metohija, and anybody could read about that. You said that you complained and that you asked to have a meeting with Bakalli. Do you remember that it was precisely Bakalli who said that the demonstrations were hostile? He termed them as being hostile himself?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did ask to meet Mahmut Bakalli to discuss the situation that was created as a result of this encyclopedia and the violence and terror committed by the Serb police against the youths and students, but he didn't come. Probably he was afraid of you, of the Serb leadership in office then. He didn't come to discuss these issues with the students.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come Bakalli was afraid of me in 1981?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in 1981, but the Albanian leadership of Kosova have never been free to operate on their own will. They had to toe your line all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that all the political structures of the times in Kosovo and Metohija assessed the demonstrations as being hostile and an act along the lines of Albanian nationalism and separatism? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them, only some. Yes, they did characterise them in the terms you said because they were under communist dictate, as I said, which was led by Belgrade. It was the central committee then which decided how these protests should be described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer my questions without going into lengthy explanations, because otherwise we're not going to be able to get through all this. I'm saying this because I do not wish to be blamed for taking up too much time myself. You said that the demonstrations took on the slogan of "Kosovo Republic." So the social and economic motive for the demonstrations were rejected straight at the beginning. You said that economic backwardness and discrimination of Kosovo and that the slogan was "Kosovo Republic"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these, as well as discontent that was created right after the Second World War, when you imposed a state of siege in Drenica, all these forces obliged us to ask for a Republic of Kosova in the context of the then Yugoslav Federation, because we thought that we were the third people in terms of size in Yugoslavia, and we were not treated equally to the others. The Montenegrins are one-third in numbers compared to us, but they had their own republic, which we didn't. I think that would have been the best solution even for Yugoslavia then, because in this way democracy would be perfected. It would be an act of philanthropy, I think, to give our people equal rights to other peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned just now the siege of Drenica after World War II. Do you know what kind of siege of Drenica that was, in fact? Just say "yes" or "no," "I do know" or "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, pretty well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And if you know it pretty well, do you know that in that locality, the Drenica locality, after the Second World War, after the fall of fascism, for several years after that, in the forests, there were bands of balijas who were collaborating -- Balistas collaborating with the German occupiers and killing people, not only around Drenica but outside Drenica as well, wherever they could get hold of somebody and leave them headless? Do you remember that? Just say "yes" or "no," "it's right" or "it's not right."

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this question with a yes or a no. Please, I'd like -- I have the right to speak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance of this is in the fact that the witness said a moment ago that an injustice had been done to the Albanian people because of the so-called siege of Drenica after the Second World War. Let me remind you that Drenica is the area around Srbica which they called Dukagjin, or rather, Drenica, and that an injustice occurred there. The truth is that part of the quisling formations who fought on the side of Hitler withdrew to the hills around that area, and for several years after that, the army made every effort to liquidate them. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far -- stop for a moment. We have to try events in the 1990s, the late 1990s. Insofar as events 50 years before are relevant, we will be the judge of that. Now, enough has been said about this matter as far as this witness is concerned. We've heard his evidence, we've heard what you say about it. Now, let us move on and more closely approximate the time we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am exclusively dealing with that particular topic, and I did not ask a single question or raise a single matter that the witness himself did not bring up, so I don't think it is in order for you to warn me and caution me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm dealing with the trial as a whole and dealing with what's relevant. But let's move on. No, don't make any comments. No. Let us -- just deal -- just kindly deal with the questions you are asked. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there should be a Kosovo Republic. Do you know that the Albanians have their original mother country, matrix state?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this? It's not going to assist us. No. Let's move on. Let's move on. Let's move on. He said that there was mention of a Kosovo Republic at these demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not say that it was mentioned; he said it was the main goal of all the activities that were undertaken by them, and the secession of Kosovo from Yugoslavia, and seizing territory away from Yugoslavia and seizing territory away from Serbia. That is what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said you were right because you were the third in size, as you say, the third ethnic group or nationality in Yugoslavia by virtue of size. Yesterday -- the day before yesterday, you said you were second in size. Today you say you were the third largest, but that's not true either. You come after the Serbs, the Croats, the Muslims and Slovenians, so you would be, in fact, by virtue of numbers, fifth in line. So you don't even operate with exact elementary figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is: Does he know about the fund for the underdeveloped, from which Kosovo and Metohija, for decades, was funded and received several times more resources and financial support than it created itself?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I didn't say that we wanted to secede from Yugoslavia but that we wanted to have a republic in the context of the Yugoslav Federation. Regarding this fund, I would like to explain to you that this was an international fund for the development of Kosova since it was the most backward country in Europe. But you misused even the international funds granted by international organisations for Kosova. It was the 1970s, I think. I was young then, but I know it was an international fund for the development of Kosova then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't even have a comment to something as ludicrous as that. There was a fund for the development of the insufficiently developed areas, a Yugoslav fund --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard his response and we can hear any evidence which you wish to call about it. Now, let us more closely approach the events in this indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am talking about what the witness spoke of, and I should like to ask you not to give me instructions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were asked the following: Did you deal with the violation of human rights against the Serbs? And you were asked this by the Prosecutor, and your answer was that there was no violation of Serb human rights and that there was no violence against Serbs in Kosovo, when asked whether there was any violence against Serbs. Now, we don't have to ascertain what you said. We all heard it. What I'm asking you about is the following: Do you know about the violence against the Serbs over the past 20 years? Let me be more precise and specific. Do you know about the killings and burnings and rapes and cutting down orchards, the destruction of churches, the digging up of cemeteries and graves and beatings up, all the other kinds of violence that have taken place these past 20 years, from 1981, when you yourself began to be in politics, the violence against the Serbs? And over 40.000 of these Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, a question. Just a moment. Let me deal with this. You've asked a series of questions in one. The first question, Mr. Kadriu, is this: Were there violations of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. human rights against the Serbs during these 20 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there were, there were very few cases, extremely few, and the Council of Human Rights and Freedoms recorded them. However, things were made up because we didn't have an Albanian in power, and the power belonged to him, and the straight apparatus and the courts were in his hands. Everything was in his hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next question is: Was there violence against the Serbs? And the various forms of violence were alleged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember any cases apart from cases that were manipulated by the Milosevic regime. I remember a case regarding a battle which was manipulated by the Serbian regime as a pretext to intervene in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's also alleged that there was destruction of churches, the digging of cemeteries, cutting down of orchards. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't heard of such things. Power was in the hands of Milosevic. Who would have dared to do such things?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask then before Milosevic, in the 1980s. Do you know about the -- those violences -- that violence, say, from 1980 to 1990? "Yes" or "no," "I do know" or "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, because at that time, the Council for Human Rights didn't exist, and there was no violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We usually count time from the days of Christ, Anno Domini, and not the Council for Human Rights. But as you lived before the time of the Council of Human Rights, do you know how many inhabitants of Kosovo and Metohija under pressure, under violence from the Albanians had to leave the province? Do you know or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't migrate because of violence but because they had much better living conditions in Serbia than in Kosova. Kosova was the poorest place in Europe. They didn't have the conditions for Serbs to live there. Why shouldn't they go to Serbia? They sold their land at a very high price to Albanians, land which they obtained before World War II in the colonisation programme, and they bought land in Serbia at half the price of the land in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm so happy that you know about the buying and selling of land and that you're well-versed in real estate, but I'm asking you, do you know how many Serbs had to leave in face of the violence and -- of the Albanians in those years? Do you know or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because the state apparatus was a Yugoslav one. It wasn't ours. It didn't belong to the Albanians. Serbia always had an influence over Kosova and controlled everything. It's absurd to think that we had a state apparatus to expel people. The movement of people was free. It was within the Yugoslav Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't need a dissertation. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also claim -- right. We've cleared up that question, but we'll come back to them later on. But you also claim that from the 1980s or perhaps the -- 1990, the Albanians were thrown out of schools, and I made a note of that here in my notes. How many mixed classes were there? How many Albanian children went to school up until 1999? Do you have any idea about this?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The removal of Albanian students from school, the classes were not mixed. They were streamed and separate although in the same school, in the same school buildings. However, the removal of Albanian pupils from their schools took place in 1988, when you came to power with so much commotion and strong feelings. You reminded the Serbian people of those myths.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll never end this questioning if you take up so much time with your answers. We'll never get through it all if you answer in this way. So may I kindly ask you to give me yes or no answers or brief explanations. Do you know about the number of students, according to the languages taught? So in Albania, tuition in Albanian and tuition in Serbian, up until the 24th of March, 1999, do you know how many students there were? I'm not talking about 1988 or God knows what year, but I'm talking about the year 1999, the beginning of 1999. Facts and figures. In Kosovo and Metohija, there was a total of, in Serbian, tuition in the Serb language in schools, a total of 45.279 students. That is students attending tuition in the Serbian language. And at that time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Stop there. Stop there. Mr. Milosevic, you rebuked the witness for taking up too much time. You're taking up time with these questions. Now, what's the question for the witness? 1999, a total of 45.279 students attending tuition in the Serbian language. That's the point. Do you know anything about that, Mr. Kadriu?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that is not my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is whether he knows that at that same time, 235.881 students were studying in the Albanian language, at the beginning of 1999, that is, 235.881.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time are you talking about? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1999. That is to say, on the eve of the war.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Albanian students were expelled from their primary schools, high schools, and their university. They were thrown out of their premises by police violence. Pupils, students were thrown out. They all studied outside their school buildings. The whole world knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No one knows that. If the world knows about it, it knows about it as propaganda. My assertion is that 235.881 students studied in the Albanian language. The witness who was here the day before yesterday, the man from Zegra, said himself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said that is not so. He said it's not so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the municipality of Vucitrn at the beginning of 1999, that is to say, your municipality - I have heard that you are now president of that municipality, or vice-president of that municipality - 12.258 students studied in the Albanian language, and in the Serb language, 39. In the municipality of Srbica that you were mentioning, 102 students in the Serb language and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him deal with one thing at a time. First of all, the allegation is made about the municipality which the witness was a resident of. Do you know anything about that, Mr. Kadriu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milosevic is supplied with erroneous information. In the village of Prelluzhe and Gojbuja, and the village of Grace, all in Vushtrri commune, mainly inhabited by Serbs, and we don't know how many school pupils there were because we are unable to go there to investigate, but UNMIK looks after school students and sees that they all go to classes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with my question whatsoever. I asked you whether you know that in the municipality of Vucitrn before the war, that is to say just before the war broke out, 12.258 Albanians studied in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just say whether you can confirm that or not, Mr. Kadriu, without making a speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not 12.000 but 14.000 students studied outside the school buildings. They were deprived of their school buildings by your police in 1991. We study in private houses. We turned our houses into schools, and even there, we weren't left in peace. Even there, they arrested dozens of teachers. You have arrested and convicted dozens of teachers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the witness from Zegra who was here the day before yesterday confirmed that children attended proper schools in school buildings, not outside school buildings, and that that school had a student body of 900, for example?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true that Albanian pupils followed classes in school premises, with the exception of some primary schools that were released for their use.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say it's not true and it is not true if that's the way you are putting it.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true. We worked in private houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There are 62 students in the high school in Vucitrn studying in the Albanian language, and at the technical school 106 students studying in the Albanian language in Vucitrn. So in addition to primary schools, I'm talking about secondary schools as well.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- the question is not clear. I don't know what answer to give because there's no question, and I don't grasp the figures. I don't know what you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic -- Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I am looking for is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have heard a lot of evidence on this question. Ultimately it will be for the Trial Chamber to determine what weight to attach to the evidence. You should move on to another area now, and as the Presiding Judge said, an area which is closer in the allegations in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you that this subject about this alleged discrimination against Albanian children, and as the first witness, Bakalli, put it, apartheid is a subject that is very close to the gravest accusations that have been levelled here. These are total lies. Hundreds of thousands of Albanian children that studied in the Albanian language are figures that are generally known, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've been told to move on, Mr. Milosevic. We have heard these arguments and no doubt we'll hear more about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that within the Geneva Conference in 1992 - in 1992, that is - the government of our country presented a proposal to overcome the problems related to education in Kosovo? The problem was that the Albanian separatists refused to give their curricula for verification to the Ministry of Education of Serbia. That's what it pertained to. And do you know that within this Geneva Conference in 1992, our government submitted a proposal that had several points? Are you aware of this proposal that was related to reaching agreement on the maximum guarantees of preserving the cultural identity of the Albanian minority? This is under point one. Point two, returning to the workplace --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. This is supposed to be a question. Now, let the witness deal with the original question. Do you know about -- Mr. Kadriu, first of all, do you know about this Geneva Conference or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This conference at Geneva, if it acted on this basis, I can only tell you that all the teachers and pupils were forced out of our schools. I don't know when this conference was held, but I can inform the accused that he -- you removed teachers and pupils from their schools with violence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is not the question you were asked. The next question is: If you know of the conference, do you know that the government put forward proposals at the conference relating to education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not true that the Serbian government took an interest in the education in Kosova. It was interested in destroying this education system. This was proved later, in the next ten years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in this programme, there was a proposal to have all Albanian teachers returned to work, all of those who had left their workplaces of their own free will, except for a very small number who had committed criminal offences? Just say yes or no, whether you know about this or not.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't answer with yes or no. Don't restrict my right to speak, otherwise I can't -- I will not answer. You have deprived me of the right to speak for ten years. Allow me to answer as I -- according to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let it be clear: This is not a political occasion; it's a trial concerned with criminal matters. It applies both to you, Mr. Kadriu, and also to you, Mr. Milosevic. Now, you were not being deprived of any rights here. The only point we make to you is to deal as quickly as you can with any questions, focusing on the question itself. You won't be restricted to yes or no unless it's an answer, but if you can answer yes or no, it will enable the work to be done more expeditiously. Now, Mr. Milosevic, ask your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the proposal related to the return of all Albanian teachers to their jobs, those who had left the workplace originally due to this problem?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1991, every year at the beginning of September we tried to enter the schools, but you prevented us. You had police contingents with bulletproof jackets and equipped with --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Don't repeat this. We heard this yesterday. Don't repeat it.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there was any such thing. Until 1997, when, together with the intervention of the Sant' Egidio organisation, something was done to return Albanian pupils to their school buildings who had been expelled by violence. There was an agreement with Rugova that was never implemented, and you deceived him twice. The agreement was signed twice. The Sant' Egidio organisation is also a witness to the fact that this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. agreement was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They are witnesses of the fact that the agreement was carried out, and it wasn't elementary or secondary education that was a problem; it was the university that, from September onwards, had received tens of thousands of square metres of space. But I'm not going to go into this any further, because we have already dealt with that here. Do you know that in this programme there was --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think now we have exhausted this topic. The Chamber has heard enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You won't let me mention schools any more at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, unless you've got some relevant question. Mr. Ryneveld -- just a moment. Mr. Ryneveld, we've spent nearly half an hour on this schools question. Now, it's true that the Prosecution raised it first, and there was evidence from the earlier witnesses about education. I think we need to reconsider whether any further evidence should be adduced on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I am not aware that we are planning on, beyond what we have done so far, to call further evidence with respect to the issue of education, except perhaps through some expert witnesses that are to be called in due course, but certainly not through these types of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The danger is that we spend a long time in a trial on matters which are strictly not part of the indictment and have very peripheral relevance to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. This evidence was led more by way of historical background as to the immediate conflict. We had no idea that this background information would be something that would take up quite this much time. So I take Your Honour's point and we will certainly take that into consideration in terms of the evidence we lead from future witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're of the view that you should move on, Mr. Milosevic. You've heard what we've said to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have just one more question, and please, it requires just a yes or no answer, and could you assist me in this. Is the witness claiming that Albanian students use the buildings of primary and secondary schools in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't use them until 1997, some even later, until KFOR came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You've answered the question. You mentioned Velika Reka and the refugees who were staying there and that this was a programme for changing the ethnic pattern. Do you know that this settlement for refugees in Velika Reka was part of the habitat programme and was assessed as one of the best of its kind by the international community and that it has a total of 84 houses? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was assessed by international community, but one thing I know, that you instrumentalised it in order to change, to alter the ethnic structure of the population of Kosova. Because if you wanted to resolve that social issue, the social problem - and I really am sorry for them - you would have settled them somewhere else where the conditions were better: in Serbia, Vojvodina, or somewhere else. The greatest density of population is in Kosova compared to all parts of former Yugoslavia, and poverty, likewise, was higher there. You didn't want to resolve the social problems, but just you used it for political ends, to change the structure of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you know that this settlement has a total of 84 houses.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number of houses, the exact number, but I know that this is what you did in other regions of Kosova, with the aim of altering the ethnic structure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this alteration of the ethnic composition, do you know that the number of refugees in Kosovo and Metohija totalled 5.000 altogether?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number of columns. I don't have information to that effect. We were unable to get any information from you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is sufficient to say that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that these 5.000 comprise 0.7 per cent of the total number of refugees who came to Serbia, that is to say, less than 1 per cent, a lot less than 1 per cent? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what number that was, but I know the purpose, the goal of that action, which was a political one, to change the ethnic structure, and I am certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then the government carried it out in the contrary way, if that was the objective, because do you know that the territory of Kosovo is 10 per cent of the total territory, and only 0.7 per cent of all refugees went to that area? Can you do the relevant math? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't make any maths here, but I'm giving you the number of buses that left Prishtina to the west as a result of the pressure and violence exerted against the Albanian population under various pretexts. There was not a single state in Europe that didn't host Kosovars that left Kosova at that time, while you kept populating it with Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear me say that there was a total of 5.000 refugees in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness says that he cannot deal with this math. On the other hand, he's dealing with the Academy of Sciences and Arts, so I don't understand how come he can't do this math that goes up to 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were arrested and interrogated because you were struggling for a Kosovo republic and because you were issuing documents on which it said "Kosovo Republic," "The Republic of Kosovo." You said that you were sentenced to 20 days in prison. Do you know that this is an administrative sentence, not a criminal sentence, and it was actually a magistrate for minor offences that had sentenced you to it? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only myself but all the Albanian teachers underwent -- or went through those doors of your police, and we were all mistreated. I'm telling you that Riza Bilali, who was the professor and the principal of the secondary school then. Qazim Azemi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked about your sentence. If it makes any difference, it's said that it was an administrative magistrate who sentenced you, or a magistrate for minor offences. Do you know who sentenced you or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were sentenced only because we taught students, for nothing else. The charges written there, it doesn't matter what was written there; they were absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, he can say whatever he wants, but you should make sure that he actually gives an answer to my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what about my question? Was this an administrative sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, what difference does that make? What difference does it make?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The difference is that he was not prosecuted in terms of having criminal charges brought against him at all. Administrative sentences are pronounced only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Kadriu, would you deal with that. Do you know it was purely an administrative sentence and not a criminal one? If you know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milosevic should know it better for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Don't comment on the evidence, please. Just answer the question. Do you know if it was a criminal sentence or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were maltreated, beaten up, and sent to prison. I don't know what name he may put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, you did in fact serve 20 days in prison for this offence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For the others, I had to pay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only myself but others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this kind of administrative sentence is pronounced for violating public law and order?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What order were we violating when we were teaching our students without being paid for that, without having the necessary conditions to do that, escaping your police, trying to dodge the police in order to educate the people? You should have subsidised the education and not ban it. Only under your government, under your power, this happened. In no place in the world -- I don't think there is any other place that this can happen. This was discrimination. We were deprived of our right to education, to educate our children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have already stated that Albanians did not use school buildings in Kosovo and Metohija. Since that is an untruth that can easily be disproved, and there are hundreds and hundreds of examples to prove that, I need no further explanation. I am asking you whether you know that these administrative sentences are pronounced if you, for example, do not pay the fine for parking in the wrong place and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've heard enough about this. We've heard what you have said, and we've heard what the witness has said. We're not going to get any further. No. No. Mr. Kadriu, there's no need to go into this. Now, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he believe then and does he believe now that the documents that they published entitled "The Republic of Kosovo," are legal documents?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were legal for us. We had our administration, our Ministry of Education, which issued such documents. And then on these documents, on these certificates, we put the marks, grades of the students. They were legal. If that were not the case, then we wouldn't have continued to teach our students, wouldn't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a sufficient answer, Mr. Kadriu. Mr. Milosevic, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you think that these documents are legal now?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly that they are. More than legal, because they had a seal. They were certified by the school teacher, principal. They were legal and issued by the Ministry of Education of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you heard of the KLA in 1991.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read in newspapers that something was being done in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You were involved in public activities, as you had put it, as far as back from the early 1990s. Do you know of the activity of the organisation of Osama bin Laden in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard about bin Laden this year. I had never heard of him before. Only during this -- I mean, when the tragedy was perpetrated against the American people, I heard about him. I never had heard about him before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is enough on that. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the Mujahedin and their atrocities in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. It's not true that there were Mujahedins in Kosova. This is a concoction of your mind, just a work of imagination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just say it's not correct or, "I don't know." Don't take up my time, please. I'm going to read to you a passage, and you'll be able to tell me whether it's correct or not: "Al Qaeda [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] some terrorist organisations that operates under its umbrella or which it supports, including..." [Interpretation] I'm going to skip over this next bit, [In English] "... Croatia, Albania," et cetera. [Interpretation] Do you consider that to be correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. That is a fiction of your imagination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. [In English] Congressional statement, Federal Bureau of Investigation. [Interpretation] Congressional statement of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. That's what this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date of it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: December 18, last year. After September 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. You can put that into evidence in due course. Meanwhile, the witness says he knows nothing of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking the witness whether the quotation I read out was correct. He said it was incorrect, that it was false, and it was the product of my imagination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now I am going to ask you the following, is this correct: [Previous translation continues]... [In English] "... Afghanistan, Bosnia, then Cechnya and Kosovo." [Interpretation] Is that passage I have quoted correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea about that. I am not here to become an advocate of Bosnia or Afghanistan. I am speaking here about Kosova. There are no Mujahedin in Kosova. This is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you what you know about their activities, not whether they exist there. That they exist has not been challenged. But what you want to say is that you know nothing of their activities; is that it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He says there were no Mujahedin in Kosovo. That's what he says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. He doesn't need that much assistance, obviously. [Previous translation continues]... [In English] "identified in Bosnia, Kosovo, Albania." [Interpretation] Is that true or is it not true, according to the knowledge you have?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I have no knowledge about other countries. Concerning Kosova, I may say that there are no Mujahedins there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The last passage I quoted was the Congressional Research Service Front Line. That was the source. You spoke about an attack on the village of Cirez. That is incorrect, because everything else you said is incorrect too. But as far as this concrete event is concerned, I want to ask you the following: Do you know on the 3rd of March, 1998, in the village of Cirez, KLA terrorists killed four policemen? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I know that there was an exchange of fire, but I know that your forces killed people there. How can I know that, who was killed there? I only know that people, civilians, even women, were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know anything about that, about the fact that four policemen were killed in a horrible manner from an ambush in the village of Cirez, before the event that you talked about? In the village of Cirez.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did your policemen want to do in the houses of the Albanian inhabitants of Cirez?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, although I'm not here to answer your questions, let me tell you that they were looking for weapons. And that is their legitimate right. And do you know that the policemen were searching for weapons and confiscated a large number of weapons, in fact? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't confiscate any weapons. They went and provoked and mistreated people in their own homes. Just to give you an example, when they searched my home, even my library was a problem for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from all this phraseology that you use with respect to maltreatment, can you speak about material, actual facts and evidence? That's what I'm asking you about. You yourself said here, and I heard you say it with my own ears, and it's probably been recorded -- not probably but it has certainly been recorded, that at the end of February the owner of the house that was mentioned by you, you said in self-defence, you used the word "self-defence," that in self-defence he had killed a policeman, a policeman who had come to search for weapons or to ask for documents and to check something out. You say that that is self-defence. Do you say that anywhere in the world to shoot a policeman that comes to arrest you, for example, not even just to search your apartment, to ask for documents, but can that be treated as self-defence anywhere in the world? Anywhere in the world, is shooting at a policeman considered being self-defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't -- just a moment. Don't deal with the broad question because that's a matter of comment, but deal, if you can, with what happened, if you can give us any more detail of what happened when the owner of the house killed a policeman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if the policeman was killed then, because it was impossible for me to get any information. I remember, however, that in Vojnik village in Drenica region, the police, accompanied by armoured cars, had gone to search a house there, an Albanian house. And then they went up to that conflict. How the conflict evolved or how it happened, I don't know, but I only know that there were casualties there in Vojnik too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And can you help us -- just one thing. Can you help us with this: To your knowledge, did the police at this time, 1998, search for weapons in the villages or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police constantly used this pretext to search all the Albanian houses and villages, every day. They maltreated people every day in their own family members' eyes, right from not only 1998, but as of 1991, this kept occurring all the time. I have the chronology of the Council for Human Rights on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not in the least bit interested in the imagined documents of this witness or his answers to the Prosecutor with respect to these fabricated documents. I am interested in material -- the material facts that he presented here, so I would like to prevail upon you to ask him to answer the questions and not go on talking about the last ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Ahmeti family lost their lives in the conflict with the KLA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go into that, you say that the documents are forged; is that right, Mr. Milosevic? Is that the allegation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me see what you said, because I wasn't able to hear. There was some noise. I wasn't able to hear. Yes. What I'm saying is -- I am claiming, in fact, that what this witness has presented on behalf of his Council for Human Rights is pure manipulation. That is what I maintain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, it's been suggested that the documents you have produced are forgeries. You should have the opportunity to deal with that and comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no document that I brought has been forged. I have brought documents from the municipal government, signed by Slobodan Doknic, and I can be responsible for each one of them. I can be responsible with my life.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not the question here. That's not the question. I'm not talking about that type of document. We'll be coming to those types of documents in due course. What I'm talking about is the information of his alleged Council for Human Rights about the sufferings of the Albanians, and I consider that they are completely -- it is a complete manipulation and nothing else. The documents he's brought here will go into those, will explain those, and easily. It's just a minor point, that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asking about the Ahmeti family. What do you say? What do you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said precisely that. He claimed that they were killed by the Serb forces. I want to say that the Ahmeti family lost their lives in a clash between the KLA and the police. That's what it was all about, and no terror on the part of Serb forces against this family. No Serb forces, as you call the police and army, undertook the maltreatment of the population. The army and the police force did not engage in any war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with that. The Ahmeti family, it's suggested that they were killed in a clash between the KLA and the police. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ahmeti family never fought with the police or the army. They were in their own home on the evening when they were surrounded. All the men were taken out of the house and were executed in the most barbaric fashion. Meanwhile, the women underwent the most appalling trauma gathered in a room. I won't talk about it. Milosevic's army and police know what they did then. Then a horror, massacre, took place. This has also been shown by non-governmental organisations from other countries who were in Kosova. Just call on their witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is an important issue. It goes directly to your case. You're saying that the Ahmeti family were in fact killed in a clash between the KLA and the police. I think you are duty-bound to put something more to the witness. Do you have any other question as to how precisely they were killed in this clash between the KLA and the police, or are you just making that as a general allegation? It would strengthen your case, it seems to me, if you were able to put more precise matters as to exactly how they were killed. Were they caught in a crossfire? Were they fighting with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are facts which exist, and the facts are that in the village of Cirez, in that particular village, on the 3rd of March, the terrorists of the KLA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put those allegations to the witness. Put them to the witness as part of your case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have put them forward, that is, that on the 3rd of March, 1998, in Cirez, the KLA terrorists killed four policemen, and that on that occasion, therefore, as a consequence of the killing, there was a further escalation of the conflict between the KLA terrorists and the police, and that the Ahmeti family was the victim of that clash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you say to that, Mr. Kadriu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am entirely convinced and sure that nobody of the members of the Ahmeti family were in the KLA. I can swear this on my life. None of them were involved in the KLA. All the men were killed, with the exception of one, who was working in the West. They were taken in their own homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not staying here -- we're not talking about the fact whether they were members of the KLA, but they were killed in a clash between the KLA and the police. But let me take it from the end, because this question was raised at the end yesterday, the killing of the so-called Gerxhaliu family, and we saw pictures here and all the explanations, attendant explanations. There are witnesses who claim that the Gerxhaliu family was precisely caught between the forces of the police and army, on the one side, and the Albanian terrorists and bandits of the KLA on the other side, and that they were sending out warnings to the Gerxhaliu family, cautioning them, saying that it was very dangerous to stay in the army because the KLA was shooting at the army precisely from that side. I have a record here, a note here, which says, according to the statement of Sali Gerxhaliu, a member of that same family, given to the Human Rights Watch, and it was published in their book of 2001. The book is called "Under Orders." It says that the investigating judge, accompanied by the police, went to the site straight away to investigate, and during the investigation, the people photographed were killed. And you're probably taking this information. And the investigating judge was a lady. She was a Serb. And when this occurred, there was serious fighting between the KLA forces and the Serb forces. The KLA was both in the village and around the village, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to stop you. You are supposed to be asking questions at this stage. Now, how is it suggested -- just a moment. How is it suggested that this family of men, women, and children were killed in this clash?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that Milosevic is a master of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Just a moment. Mr. Milosevic, how is it suggested that this family that we've been dealing with, and the photographs of which of the bodies we have seen, and the position, how is it suggested that they were killed in the clash with the KLA? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, but you didn't let me read out this note that I received. It says: The army of Yugoslavia and the KLA were fighting. They were in and around the village, that is to say, the members of the KLA, and while they were leaving the house from which they opened fire on the army, they liquidated the Gerxhaliu family; the KLA did. Now, how they took in and brought out the bodies, that's another question. So in the same book - and the book is called "Human Rights --" - and it says on the same day, at 4.00 in the morning, he heard two NATO explosions which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's far enough. You've heard the suggestion which has been made, Mr. Kadriu. Do not comment upon it, or the source, but help us with this: As far as you know, is there any truth in that suggestion? And can you assist us with any more detail about how this event happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a mockery, a mockery of the victims, and he should be ashamed of himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's precisely what is not going to assist. Now, can you just deal with the matter factually, please. Now, you've heard the suggestion. You say it's not true. Can you assist us at all with any of the detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 31st of May, in the early hours of the morning, military and police forces concentrated on the Rashica neighbourhood, not more than 200 metres away, went down and entered among the family of Selatin Gerxhaliu and then committed a crime, executing the entire family. There were no forces of the KLA in Studime e Poshtme because that was where Serbian forces were concentrated. This is the truth. You might know the point where the Serbian forces were concentrated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the source of your information on this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In this case, in his own house -- not very far from his house, Shukri Gerxhaliu was there - and he should be coming here as a witness - with his wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You got this information from him; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and from many others who know about this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The microphone has just been switched on. You forgot to switch it on after you had switched it off. Now we have heard an absolutely fantastic assertion here, and for purposes of clarity and for the record, I would like to ask another question to make things clear. The witness is saying that the police entered the house and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. killed, in cold blood, the Gerxhaliu family, and then sent for the investigating judge to come and ascertain what they had done. Or perhaps the other variant is the following: that the police entered, saw that the family had been killed, and called the investigating judge to see the crime that had taken place over a family. What do you, gentlemen, as men of the law, think is more logical, particularly in view of the explanation we've just been given?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question is: Does he claim that the police came and killed the family and then called the investigating judge to come and ascertain how the family had been killed? Is that what he's saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Kadriu, if the investigating judge was called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether he was called or not, but this was an obstruction by the Serbian military and police which they had done before. They would commit a crime and then call for the judge. This was a form of obstruction for certain intentions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good, that. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you have claimed on several occasions that there was no violence committed against the Serbs, that is to say, you have claimed that this false indictment claims that it is the Serbs who are the culprits, do you know how many terrorist attacks were performed in Kosovo and Metohija from 1991 until June 1999?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about attacks, because the state apparatus was in your hands. I don't know. Things were staged, improvised, for certain purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know anything about that? Well, how, then, did you think you would protect human rights if you don't know about terrorist attacks? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear of the fact that in 1998 alone there were 1.885 terrorist attacks in that year alone? Just in that year, 1998, when the terrorists were assisted by the German services and other services and when they started all this. One thousand, eight hundred and eighty-five attacks in 1998. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As you weren't interested in what was going on and being done against the Serbs, the police, and the army, or anybody else, and you say that you were interested what was happening to the Albanians, do you know the following: How many terrorist attacks there were on citizens of Albanian ethnicity? Do you know how many of those were performed in Kosovo and Metohija against Albanian citizens?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that attacks on Albanian citizens were made by your army, escorted by your secret police in a jeep which -- of a dark olive colour, who killed people on the streets, just as my workmate Skender Bllaca was murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we're going to adjourn now. We'll adjourn now for quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So my question was does he know about the crimes of the KLA terrorists committed against the Albanians, and I did not get an answer.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered that question that during 1997, 1998, the Serb secrete police moved about and around the place with dark-coloured cars and killed the people. And among these people who were killed was also my workmate Skender Bllaca, whose photo is here with me. And I can tell you about his CV, if you wish. The police killed them at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, the question you were asked was whether you know whether the KLA members committed crimes against Albanians. Just -- you can say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not true. These crimes were committed by Serb secret police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please stick to the question and simply answer it yes or no. Thank you. You may go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My specific question in the context of these crimes of the terrorists against the Albanians was what I asked you. There were also inter-party killings. That's well-known. This was committed by Hashim Thaci against Rugova's supporters. Does he know of the following incident: The killing of Rexhep Bajrami, Rexhep Bajrami from the village of Cecelija, who was an activist of Rugova's in that village and who was killed on orders of the local KLA commander whose name is Krasniqi? Otherwise, he is the uncle of Hashim Thaci. The killing of Rexhep Bajrami was ordered by him only because Bajrami would not take Rugova's picture off the wall. Does the witness know about this event in the context of his work in the field of human rights?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this name "Rexhep Bajrami" does not exist in Vushtrri. I don't know anyone by that name to have been killed. Probably the information the accused has is wrong. There isn't such a case. I can say it in full authority. Not in my municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does he know that in 1998 there were 327 terrorist attacks against members of the Albanian national minority who were loyal to the Republic of Serbia? In 1998, 327 attacks.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't believe that there were Albanians who were loyal to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, for example, that a member of the Executive Council, that is to say, the provincial government, an Albanian, Faik Jashari, when you were expelling Serbs from Kosovo, stated: "The columns of Serbs from Kosovo have been joined by 30.000 Albanians as well, those loyal to the Republic of Serbia." Do you remember this statement made by Faik Jashari, an Albanian who was a member of the provincial government at the time when Serbs were expelled from Kosovo after UNMIK and KFOR came?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there is any Faik Jashari in my municipality, so I don't know anything about such an absurd statement. I don't know where you get such statements, such false statements. There isn't anyone by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that several Albanians were members of the provincial government during the years of 1998, 1999, and during the war?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. No. I don't remember anything. I don't remember of such a person being the member of the provincial government. Maybe some quislings there may have been, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know about Faik Jashari? Was he an Albanian? Is he an Albanian? What is he?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time to hear such a name, in this very court. I say it in full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You never saw him, not even on television, or you never heard him over the radio? You don't know of him at all?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say it in full competence, I have never seen or never heard anything about this man. It's the first time for me to hear it, in this very court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about Albanians who were members of the delegation of Serbia at the negotiations in Rambouillet? Have you heard of them? Have you seen them on television?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Serb delegation was there, but I don't know its composition. I know that some leaders were there, but I was never interested to find out more about that composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about another member of the government, also an Albanian? There were a few of them. I'm not going to mention them all right now, and Xhafer Gjuka is the one I'm referring to now. Your members of the KLA slit his throat after the members of UNMIK came to Pec. Have you heard of him? Have you heard of Xhafer Gjuka?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard of Xhafer Gjuka. I am from Vushtrri municipality, and this is the first time to hear about this man too. I'm afraid you have wrong information, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I knew Xhafer Gjuka personally, so this bit of information I have certainly is not wrong. I'm just asking you whether you know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says he doesn't. No need to say any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about hundreds of kidnapped civilians by the Albanian terrorists, and do you know of the consequences of these kidnappings? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Albanian civilians being kidnapped you are talking about? I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what is unclear about this. As far as I know, everything I'm saying is being interpreted to you in Albanian. I'm talking about kidnapped civilians, civilians who were kidnapped by the KLA, and many were killed later as well. Do you know anything about that? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of such a thing. This is the first time for me to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember the attack on the police station in Prelluzhe on the 28th of August, 1998?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't any attacks mounted there. This village is inhabited mainly by Serbs. I don't remember anything, but I can tell you that there hasn't been any such case, otherwise, I would have remembered that. How could Albanians enter a Serb-inhabited village?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim, you claim as a matter of fact that in Prelluzhe there were no Albanians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the vicinity of Prelluzhe, yes, there were Albanians, but in the village per se, there weren't Albanians. Beyond the river, there were some houses, which were all burnt down by Serb police and citizens of Prelluzhe. They were the first houses to be burnt in 1998. Even to this day, the Albanians have not returned to those houses in the vicinity of Prelluzhe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you claim that there were no Albanians in Prelluzhe, how do you explain, for example, that in 1990, in 1990, the president of the Executive Council of Albania, a man by the name of Xhaferi signed a decision transferring Albanian children from the school in Prelluzhe to a school 50 metres away in the village of Donja Stanovci? Since there were more of them there, they would attend school together. How do you explain that document, for example?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in 1998, if I remember right. I was doing my military service then. And I recall when on television I saw the coverage of the meeting held between -- among the Serb citizens whereby they asked that all Albanians leave the vicinity of Prelluzhe where they were living, as well as the children should leave the school. This is the first time that Albanians started to be evicted from schools in Kosova. The Albanian students, I mean. I remember also the speeches, the extraordinary address you gave then, in which you called for a Greater Serbia, and so on and so forth. You would just be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Don't go on. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see this speech of mine, the speech that I made? Where did I take this speech?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well. I said I was doing my military service, and then we had to follow all your speeches. Your officers forced us to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did I make this speech? You said that you had to follow my speeches. Where did I make that speech?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You made that speech in Belgrade. We were obliged to see it on television. And your officers started to take pride in you after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did I say in this speech?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well you saying that either Serbia will lie from Mali i Gjoshit to Gjergjeli or it will not exist at all, and I am certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Serbia does begin from the border with Hungary and it ends at the border with Macedonia. I don't understand what you tried to say. That I said that Serbia would be in Macedonia as well: Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what you said then, in 1998. That was your claim then, not only about Macedonia, but you wanted to have a Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Of course this is not true, and that is not what it says there. But this is just as incorrect as other things you've been saying here, so I'm not going to engage in a debate with you on that. Let me continue from where I had broken off. You do not know anything about the killings of Serbs, Albanians, civilians, policemen, kidnappings; you know nothing about any of this, right? On the contrary, your assertion is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt with this. Now, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know about what happened on the 19th of September, 1998, in the village of Makmal, on the road between Glogovac and Serbia, the attack against policemen, when three policemen were wounded?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of this case, because I am from Vushtrri municipality, so I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Excellent.
