And do you know, then, of the attack in the village of Oshlan, in the municipality of Vucitrn, on the 22nd of September, 1998, when the police were attacked by automatic rifles and hand-held rocket launchers, and when Milos Radic, a policeman, was killed? Do you remember that incident? On the 22nd of September, 1998, the municipality of Vucitrn, the village of Oshlan. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 22nd of September, 1998 -- and in my evidence yesterday, I informed the Court that all the villages on both sides of the mountains of Cicavica were attacked by police and military forces. This was a very Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. extensive offensive, involving both the police and the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yesterday, you yourself, as you were explaining something else, that the KLA was stationed - these are your words - stationed in the area of Cicavica. That is what you said yourself yesterday, of course, not in this respect, but while you were explaining other things, but that is also recorded. So the KLA was stationed in the area of Cicavica. How can you then speak about attacks on villages and villagers?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't deny what I said. I said that the KLA had various positions in this area. However, the attack by the police and military was on the civilian population. Civilians were killed, and I have their names here with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the army and the police went to shoot at civilians there, not the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KLA was not a terrorist army; it was a liberation army for Kosova. And you killed civilians there, and I have their names here. Not only killing them, but mutilating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for massacres, we know whose specialty that is. That is why I asked you whether you knew about Al Qaeda branches in Kosovo. It is known very well who massacres and who cuts heads off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have dealt with that. Now, this is not going to assist the Trial Chamber. What is the next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that very same day, the 22nd of September, 1998, there were several attacks against the police in the village of Oshlan, that is to say, between 1200 and 1500 hours, when two policemen were wounded, Marko Galo [phoen] and Milutin Ivkovic in the village of Oshlan, that is to say, on the 22nd of September, 1998, in the municipality of Vucitrn, that is to say, your municipality?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, on the 22nd of September, the offensive started against 27 villages to the east of Cicavica, and other villages beyond Cicavica, and this offensive caused more than 200 people executed, all of them civilians with the exception of one, who was a soldier of the KLA. With one exception. The others were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in the same village, on the 23rd, that is to say, the next day, again the police were attacked. Slavoljub Ivkovic and Micko Vranic were the victims. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police were not attacked, because these villages are mainly inhabited by Albanians. But it was the Serbian police and military surrounded these villages on both sides of Cicavica and kept them as if in quarantine until the 25th of September, until they were freed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your claim is that in all these incidents, on the 22nd, on the 23rd of September, when all these policemen that I have mentioned were killed or wounded, that all of this was actually in the police campaign against civilians?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there were Serbian soldiers or policemen wounded or killed, as you claim. However, I do know that the Serbian army and police exercised terror against 27 villages in Vushtrri municipality and other villages in Gllogovc municipality, and this led to the massacre of many civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that the KLA did not kill anyone, did not wound anyone, that it was the police attacking civilians and even attacking and killing themselves.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vukovar too, and in Srebrenica, civilians killed each other, according to your logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, according to your logic. That is your assertion, that this was all done by the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the same day, on the 23rd of September, in the village of Dubofc, Radoje Cvetkovic, a policeman, was seriously wounded in this series of attacks against the police?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that on this day, the 24th, you executed 13 young men and elderly people and killed a woman, and among those people executed, three were pupils of the school where we worked. Fourteen we buried in the village of Galice. They were all civilians, and I can say this with total confidence. Their bodies were also mutilated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who killed them?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your police and army. Your police and army, led by Janic, who led the offensive masked with Vucina Janic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not the answer to the question you were asked. And at this time, Mr. Milosevic, I understand you may put questions to this witness regarding your case to a certain extent, but in terms of time we are given today, I'd like to advise you to concentrate more on factual issues which appeared, emerged, during the examination-in-chief. As you were told yesterday, we are going to finish with the witness today, so we have not more than two hours from now on. And you yourself said that you have some questions regarding the documents this witness presented yesterday, so why don't you start with some specific questions regarding those kind of matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is precisely concrete issues that I'm addressing, specific ones, because it's not true that the army or the police committed any crimes whatsoever, which is something that this false indictment and the witness brought in by this false indictment is trying to show. But, yes, let me move on to the specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You described as a massacre of civilians --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, they were extraterrestrials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, let the accused finish his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the events that took place in the village of Prekaz when a bandit group of Adem Jashari died, and that's a very good example of how killers and terrorists are being proclaimed to be civilians. And you yourself said here, and it says so in your written statement as well, that Adem Jashari was overcome, overpowered when he ran out of ammunition. Therefore, you yourself here in this place quite clearly indicate the fact that Jashari and his group fought against the police and shot at the police. And as you know, there were several tens of them in numbers. Is that true or is it not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Adem Jashari defended his own home and defended his own doorstep. I do know that. But I also know another truth, and that is that in Adem Jashari's house, women, girls, and children, were massacred. Sixty-three graves were dug, mainly of civilians. I do not know -- I do not deny that Adem Jashari defended his own home, but you attacked it. You attacked him in his own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Serbs and Albanians Adem Jashari killed and looted with his band of men before the police came to arrest him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just deal with the question which is put or should be put in this way: It's suggested that Adem Jashari had a band of men. So the first question is this: Did he have a band of men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that day when Adem Jashari was killed alongside his family in his home, there were women, children, and elderly people who were massacred. There was a large family and a lot of them were killed, with the exception of one small girl who survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did he have a band of men who looted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. It's not true that he looted. He fought a liberation struggle. These were people defending their own hearths from Chetnik forces coming from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When the police came to arrest him, do you know that the police did not shoot but asked them to come out and to surrender themselves, to give themselves up to the police?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I'm glad that you are aware of this because it shows that you knew everything that was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I saw a report about it. And the witness that testified here before you criticised the procedure undertaken by the police, that it only gave two hours to Jashari and his band to surrender. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard this for the first time today, because all the people who were surrounded were executed in the most barbaric manner. Only a small girl survived. They were also mutilated. Who could survive to tell the tale?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not true that only one small girl survived, because in those two hours, during those two hours, a number of family members managed to leave the house, and Jashari and his members, his band of men -- you refer to them as a family, but of course there are other instances in the world where bands are referred to as families, but anyway, Jashari and his band opened fire on the police force from heavy machine-guns and automatic weapons. Several tens of automatic weapons were used to fire on the police. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There were two questions there, two questions. The first question is: Do you know if any family members managed to leave the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that anybody got out. Everybody was executed except for this girl who survived and is still among us today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can take a look at the report about the event, but it is correct not only that they managed to leave but the police appealed to everybody to come outside, to leave the house and to give themselves up to the police. Now, do you know that he, that is to say, he killed a nephew from behind, in the back, because he wanted to surrender to the police and he thought that this was being -- that he was being a traitor and therefore shot him in the back, the son of his uncle?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true, because you executed the entire Jashari family apart from this small girl who survived by chance. This is a fiction of your imagination. And you were involved in this event yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We are not contesting the fact that Jashari was killed in the clash with the police. That is not being put into question. But obviously from what you're saying, another thing is not being put into question and that is that he didn't want to be arrested but he fired, he shot, together with all the members of his band of men or bandits. Do you think that the policemen should have killed -- kamikaze policemen, for Jashari to kill them first and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is enough. It is not disputed that shots were fired. The question is how and in what circumstances. Mr. Milosevic, how do you suggest - so the witness can deal with it - that the 60 members of the family came to die? Is it suggested that they were killed in gunfire, in exchange of gunfire? Is that the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. It's common knowledge, a generally known fact. You don't know what the house looks like. And I read the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It's -- just -- let the witness deal with the suggestion. The suggestion is that this family were killed, 60, in an exchange of fire or the like. Yes. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't deny that Adem Jashari was a member of the KLA. However, Adem Jashari's family were killed. They were executed by the Serbs, including girls, children. I saw mutilated children with my own eyes. How can this be excused, killing women, two elderly men in the family, almost 80 years old? They were -- according to Milosevic, they were on some barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They weren't at a barricade but in a reinforced house, and you yourself said that from that house they shot at the police.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in their own house. They were asleep when they were surrounded by the Serbian police and army. They were asleep when you surrounded them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, what's the source of your information about this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was early in the morning when Adem Jashari's family was surrounded. Not only the family but the whole neighbourhood in Prekazi i Poshtem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you were not there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then they were executed. No, I wasn't there, but we saw from a distance, perhaps a few kilometres away, but I know that there were three rings of encirclement. It was true that we couldn't go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you told us you saw the bodies. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But what sort of age were the bodies that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were all of all ages, Your Honour. I saw the corpses when the police had taken them to a warehouse of building materials while the house of the Jashari family in Prekaz was still surrounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you actually witness how they were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. How they were killed? No. But I saw the corpses. They were burned, mutilated, and they had been executed by gunshots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you go with Mr. Barani there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I went with several human rights representatives from Vushtrri, and there I met Mr. Barani, who was filming, and the representatives of the Human Rights Council from Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just said a moment ago that you were two or three kilometres away, watching the event. How long did you watch it go on for?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there several times, because this went on. And I had to go back to -- to return to Vushtrri to report what I had seen with my own eyes. I saw smoke. There were gunshots, anti-aircraft artillery firing. For three days on end, they were subjected to Serbian artillery fire in the Jashari family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say three days? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me it was three days. You kept the house surrounded even later. Even later, it was kept besieged. There were victims who were drawn -- who were pulled out of the ruins, out of the ruins of burned houses, and they still haven't been identified to this day these members of the Jashari family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So according to your testimony just now, the police surrounded the house and for three days fought with a fortified -- with the fortified forces of Jashari, is that it? And there were a lot of policemen, as you yourself said. How large should the forces be, then, that were shooting at the police if the police needed three days to overcome them? How large were those forces, then?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were executed on the first day, but you kept the house under siege because you had to prepare the minutes of what happened, which you then presented to the media. You kept the house encircled for certain purposes so that when you presented it to the international opinion, you had a version for that, a false version of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in your opinion, how long did this fighting go on between the Jashari group and the police? How long?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say for sure how long it lasted, but I know that they were attacked early morning, and people were killed also early morning. But you kept the house under siege. All the neighbourhood, in fact, preventing anyone from going near until you took the corpses to this construction materials warehouse in the vicinity of the Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This is quite clear. Your position is quite clear in that respect, and you yourself were not able to deny the existence of fighting between the police and this group of bandits of his. You said that after these events --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not any group of bandits. Excuse me, Your Honours. There wasn't any group of bandits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We have the evidence on this matter. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Ask your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you switch my microphone on again. Ah, it's switched on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, usually everywhere in the world a group fighting against the police force is referred to as a group of bandits, probably just not here. You said that the inhabitants were escaping, were fleeing to Vucitrn, and that they were fleeing from the terror. Do you mean that they were fleeing from the police terror or were they fleeing from the area where there was shooting going on, like in this particular incident that we have just been referring to a moment ago ad infinitum until we reach some truths?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: How couldn't people resist from fleeing when your army and police began to shell their houses? And before doing that, they -- along with shelling their houses, they started to evict the inhabitants forcibly, then to set fire to their houses and deport them from -- away from Vushtrri towards Macedonia and Albania. That was the underlying philosophy of your army and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's a good thing that you're a philosopher, but I'd like to remain with material facts.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a philosopher. I never studied philosophy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we do not need these comments. Would you kindly refrain from them. Now, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read out a passage, and it is the following. As you are talking about expulsion in 1998, I'm going to read you the following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, to be fair, you must say where this passage comes from. Give us the context.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I will say that once he answers my question. I will reveal it straight away. But I don't want to tell him in advance where the passage comes from. I want to ask him the question first, to ask him about it - I assume that's my right - and then I'll disclose the source later on. He claimed that it was not true that I told him in advance that the official congress testimony of the Federal Investigation Bureau of the American Congress, he probably said that -- would probably say that that was not true either, that it was a fiction of my imagination, had I not quoted it to him. This is the passage. I'm not going to hide the source. Of course not. [In English] [As read] "Explicit political persecution linked to Albania ethnicity is not verifiable. The east of Kosovo is still not involved in armed conflict. Public life in cities like Pristina, Urosevac, Gnjilane, et cetera, has in the entire conflict period continued on a relatively normal basis. The actions of the security forces not directed against the Kosovar Albanians as an ethnically defined group but against the military opponent and its actual or alleged supporters."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your opinion; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they have written there, but I do know that your army and police killed about 15.000 civilian people, Mr. Milosevic. I don't know who wrote that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about your fabricated interpretations. What I'm asking you: Is what I have read out correct or not? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. Your police and army drove people out and deported them with violence, and killed them in so doing, and then collected them in cities as of the 1st of April. It drove them away from these cities too, forcibly. Some it killed, some it evicted forcibly to Macedonia and to Albania. That is the truth. One million people were deported to Macedonia, Albania, and other European countries. You did ethnic cleansing of Kosova. This is what you did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I should like to request that my questions be answered, because we're wasting valuable time, which I will be short of. I don't mind how long the witness is going to answer, but I do mind that he is being repetitious. He is repeating and repeating like a parrot the same thing, that it is the Serbs who are the criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what I read out, in your opinion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no point going over that. He's effectively denied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. This is an intelligence report from the foreign office, January 12th, 1999, [In English] Court of Trier, [Interpretation] to the administrative court of Trier. And I'm going to read you another passage: [In English] "As laid out in the previous status report, the KLA has resumed its position after the partial withdrawal of the security forces in October 1998, so it once again controls broad areas in the zone of conflict. Before the beginning of spring 1999, there were still clashes between the KLA and security forces, although this has not until now reached the intensity of the battles of spring and summer 1998." [Interpretation] Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the expansion of KLA, you might wish to call the KLA commander. I am here to testify to the atrocities perpetrated by your army and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This is once again a report [In English] March 15, 1999, to administrative court Mainz. [Interpretation] I'll skip this, because you say you are not a KLA commander. As you spoke about the Kosovo Verification Commission of the OSCE, do you know that there was a commission of the federal government for cooperation with this Verification Mission and that all the incidents that occurred in the space of those several months while the Verification Mission was on site, that minutes were kept between the federal government of Yugoslavia and the Verification Commission, that is to say, the government body for cooperation with the Verification Mission, that minutes existed? Do you know that? Do you know that that kind of assertation of the incidents and the minutes made by the Verification Commission and the federal government commission, that a report was written in connection with each of the incidents that took place? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there is, but if there is, I don't have any information from the OSCE about that. Of course, its work was to draft a report on the situation that prevailed then, when it was in Kosova as well as in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but do you know that -- what you say during your testimony, there is practically nothing -- nothing is contained of that in the reports, or rather, the minutes that were compiled between the Verification Mission of the OSCE and the representatives of the commission of the federal government for cooperation with this commission in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness says he knows nothing about these minutes, so any questions along these lines is purely a matter of comment. The witness cannot help us. He's given his evidence and that's all he can do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll have to sift through my questions and cut down on them, because the witness doesn't know anything about this, as you say. But I should like to draw your attention to the very clear contradictions that occurred at different points during the witness's testimony. First of all, he spoke about the stationing of the KLA in the area of Cicavica and the activities, but on the other side now, of the police and army in the Cicavica area, which is undoubtedly a conflict between the KLA and the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is not the occasion for you to make those comments. You will have an opportunity at the end of the case to address us on contradictions. You must put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that by asking these questions, all these inconsistencies are being established. I do not have the opportunity or possibility to make a record of all the inconsistencies, because these are sheer, unadulterated lies here, and cooperation with this false indictment and the witnesses that that indictment brings forward. Because the question arises is: Who is doing the killing in Kosovo now, when there are no Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just put a question. No more speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as you're not going to let me explain this, let me ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is doing the killing in Kosovo now when there's no Serb army or police force there? Who is doing the killing in Kosovo now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no relevance that the Tribunal can see in that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us go back to Vucitrn. I want to know, because he deals in human rights, whether he knows that after UNMIK and KFOR arrived, precisely in his municipality, the municipality of Vucitrn, 27 Serbs were killed. Does he know about that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that there are no Serbs in Vushtrri municipality. There are three villages mainly inhabited by Serbs. As to the killings Milosevic is referring to, I don't know that, because that is the responsibility of UNMIK to control the situation and to take records of what is happening. I am a professor at the secondary school and I am no longer president of the Council for Human Rights and Freedoms. There is someone else who is in that position now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This did not happen now; it happened when KFOR and UNMIK came, and at that time you were chairman of the council. Do you know that on the 18th of May of 1999, where there is a forest by the village of Buzh [phoen], that the KLA killed six Serbs on a tractor who went out to the forest to cut wood: Slobodan Brajkovic, the father of three children; Slavujko Miletic, father of three children; Predrag Zdravkovic, father of three children; Slavisa Zdravkovic, a young man; Milovan Zdravkovic, father of four children; and Svetislav Zivkovic? Are you aware of this? Are you aware of the killing of these people who were going to the forest to cut wood? They were in a tractor.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of May, I was in prison, in the prison of your army and police. They took me to prison. How could I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could you know about all sorts of events that you testified about here and that you said that you had heard about, that they told you about them, that you coordinated work in this area, et cetera, in the very same way, therefore?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you: At that time I was not -- I was in prison, and we couldn't get hold of any information there. We were cut off from the rest of the world, rounded by your forces. We didn't have access to any information, any newspapers, so how could I know that, in prison? I didn't know of what happened to my family until after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you didn't hear about that, Mr. Kadriu, after you came out of prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 18th of May, the date the accused has mentioned, I hadn't heard of anything happened on that day, and I'm sure nothing happened on the 18th of May. I know that when the OSCE was at Mijalic, when they were still present in the town, someone from this village who was in the Yugoslav army committed an act of sabotage and fled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to make an effort. I'm going to digress now, because I see that you keep restricting my time, and I have to go back to these documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You brought here a considerable number of documents. Before I move on to these documents, I would like to ask you something. As far as I could notice here, at least six times during your testimony you said that your documents burned. So these documents of yours that did not burn are quite worthless. We will establish that. And it so turns out that only documents that pertain to certain crimes burned. And now documents that relate to potatoes and things like that did not burn down, and on the other hand, documents relating to crimes did burn down. How could these documents be separated in this way? You refer to this at least six times, that all your documents burned down except for the documents relating to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. potatoes, purchases of cars, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is: How come these documents that are worthless he did manage to salvage and the documents that he had relating to crimes and that he mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The question is: It's suggested that your other documents were burnt but you managed to salvage these ones. Now, can you give us your evidence about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the technical secretary of the Council of Human Rights and Freedoms concealed the overwhelming majority of the council's documents in a house that was later burned. I can also give you the name of the secretary of the council, while these documents which Milosevic is trying to cover up were taken from the office of the municipality where the Serbian administration worked. They were taken after the war. There were very few documents that survived. There were some that were in copies that a colleague had but very few. And I would be very happy if I had all these documents at my disposal that I had before the war because they would help me a lot. It's my misfortune here that I don't have these documents, but the Council for Human Rights and Freedoms has the time scale of all the acts of violence, and I brought a copy here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to ask you about these documents, because the Prosecutor has presented them so pompously here, worthless documents, and he cannot make up for their value. What do you prove by a list of members of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Vucitrn when there is a crisis and when there has to be a Crisis Staff of the municipality of Vucitrn? What do you prove with a list of the members of the Crisis Staff? By the way, I see up here in the heading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a question for the witness. He simply produced the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he brought it with some intention, some purpose. I'm asking you what he's trying to prove with this document. That a Crisis Staff exists? It exists in every municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It's not a matter for the witness to deal with it. Now what is the next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does he know that this staff was organised for the Civil Defence, for evacuation, for taking care of the population, for providing food supplies, water, electricity, public goods, for taking care of the livestock that was killed, that all of that is the duty of the Crisis Staff? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Crisis Staff which was formed in 1998 was called a Staff for Police and Military and Civilian Issues. I also have other documents, and if the Court requires, I can show you that this is what it said. It was formed in order to replace all the other authorities that had previously existed and created a state of emergency. It was responsible for everything, even for the potatoes that Milosevic mentioned. Meanwhile, we know what it did to a civilian population where people are concerned. This Crisis Staff is responsible for everything. It was a supreme body which had direct contacts with the top of the pyramid where the accused was. In the Crisis Staff, there were -- there was also the police chief, Vucina Jacnicevic [phoen], who is a member of the Crisis Staff and the former chairman of the municipality; Slobodan Doknic and others who took responsible for the tiniest things, not to mention the main issues. If you want other documents, I have them here in my bag and I can give them to you, where you see written "Staff for Military, Civilian, and Police Affairs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, among the many things that you said, there is one that interests me in particular, that the Crisis Staff had contact with the top of the pyramid where the accused was. Would you like to clarify that? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. In 1998, there was a Municipal Assembly composed mainly of Serbs. From June 1998, this Municipal Assembly was turned into a Crisis Staff for military, police, civilian, and humanitarian affairs. All the Municipal Assembly's responsibilities were taken over, and these responsibilities were passed to this staff which was for military, police, and civilian affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let it be quite clear. It is correct that the Municipal Assembly did not work properly. It is true that they did not work properly because of well-known squabbling amongst the Serbs themselves and that this is why this council was appointed. And this temporary, provisional council appointed the Crisis Staff precisely for the protection of civilians and precisely because of the issues that I refer to. That is why these documents are totally worthless from the point of view of what he's trying to prove. Please. This is a question I'm putting now: The list of certificates for persons that were engaged in the Territorial Defence of Vucitrn, and then there is the name and surname and then the time period in which people were engaged, for one month, from the 25th of March until the 25th of April. That is to say, people who were engaged to transport food supplies, different materials in their own vehicles. This is mobilisation by the Crisis Staff. What is being proved by this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is being proved is what -- what -- what is being proved is what the document states. What the weight to be attached to it or its importance is a matter for the Trial Chamber in due course. The witness can't answer it. He's here simply to say that he's found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And it will be perfectly open to you in your closing address to say to us that it is a worthless document, but this is not the occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the occasion to the extent to which the Prosecution attaches - how should I put this? - top importance to this by presenting these documents on the overhead projector and things like that. They show a list of persons who were mobilised to transport in their own vehicles various supplies that were needed by the civilians. For example --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you another thing. This decision of the Crisis Staff, that a person who is authorised to use the financial resources of the Crisis Staff, do you know what this that you call the order issuing authority is? That is the person who actually has been authorised to use financial resources from a certain bank account for a certain company. This person has the right to sign cheques, to make payments, and who is therefore responsible for the use of these financial resources. So what is wrong with that? If the president of the municipality is the one who is authorised to use financial resources --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is being proved by this kind of thing? The Prosecution presented this so pompously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not for the -- not for the witness to answer. We can hear argument about it in due course. What you seem to be saying, though, is this: First of all, you say the document's a forgery, and then you're saying even if it isn't a forgery, it's unimportant. That seems to be what you're saying. Have you got now any questions now for the -- other questions for the witness? Because if not, we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why are you making it impossible for me to put questions to this witness concerning documents that he brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What I am telling you is that it's not for him to say what importance the documents have. That is for the Prosecution in due course. He has merely brought the documents. Now, you can ask him questions about the documents, you can ask him about the contents, but what you can't do is deliver a speech on the importance or unimportance of them. That's a matter of the weight of evidence about which we'll hear in due course. Now, we'll adjourn now. Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have limited my time to -- of cross-examination up until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said 1.00. 1.15 is not that suitable because I have a visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge May, I apologise. I don't know how you're going to continue with the trial and how you lead it, that's up to you, but I too wanted to raise some vital issues which are linked to many of the problems that have to do of matters of substance and not what the witness brought up, and I would need at least half an hour, 25 minutes to half an hour, to do what I consider necessary for me to be able to take part in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can sit until quarter past. Mr. Ryneveld, any re-examination you anticipate?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had anticipated two questions. However, given circumstances, I thought I could perhaps deal with that in closing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we're going to do is to deal with the limited amount of time. We -- Mr. Milosevic, we can sit until 1.15. We shall allow the amicus to cross-examine up to half an hour. No more, of course. It's up to you how long you choose to take. If you go until five to one, which you may if you wish, the amicus will then have to deal with questioning in 20 minutes. We have to balance the time between the various parties. If you want to finish earlier, of course, you'll get away earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's a sort of blackmail, because you said we would be working until 1.00 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's up to you. Now, I suggest if you want to ask further questions, you do so now and we waste no further time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you do not have the right to restrict cross-examination, according to your own Rules, and the Prosecution had much longer for his examination. And here we're talking about a witness who has been speaking untruths from beginning to end, so we cannot get through this in 15 minutes, even under this kind of pressure, even if I defer the visit that you have allowed me after having curtailed it the first time. So I think that we could continue until 1.00 today and to continue on Monday when you say so, in the normal working hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have made our ruling. The practice of the Tribunal allows Trial Chambers, where extensive time is being taken up, to limit time of examination and cross-examination. Now, what's your next question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case you have restricted the cross-examination but not the examination-in-chief. You allowed one and a half hours more for the examination-in-chief, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is, and then the witness can give us yes or no answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood you to be conferring and that I'm not to continue with my questions until you finish conferring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about when Ljubomir Knezevic, a correspondent of Radio Pristina and correspondent of Politika, the newspaper Politika, was kidnapped while on duty and taken to the village of Likovac at Cicova [phoen], and after a lot of torture, cutting off his ears and fingers, he expired on the 6th of May, 1999 [as interpreted]? Have you heard about that event?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a village by the name of Nikolic does not exist. I am afraid you've got wrong information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Ljubomir Knezevic, not Ljubomir Nikolic. The man's name was Ljubomir Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I'm not talking about a village. I'm talking about Ljubomir Knezevic from Vucitrn, who was a correspondent of Radio Pristina and the Politika newspaper. I don't know what they're interpreting in Albanian to you, but I think I was clear. Ljubomir Knezevic is the first and last name of the correspondent of Radio Pristina and correspondent for newspaper Politika. He was from Vucitrn. He was kidnapped and taken to the village of Likovac at Cicova, and after a lot of torture, which I described, expired in his misery on the 6th of May, 1995 [as interpreted]. Do you know anything about him?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date are you talking about? Because on the 2nd of May I was in prison, so I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But do you know anything about the death of this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I was in prison then. I returned in June, after the war ended, on the 19th of June. Sorry, 29th of June. At the end of June, I returned from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know, then, that in Likovac, generally, there was a well-known prison where many Serbs were killed, not only from the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Vucitrn municipality but many others too?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard of any prison there. I know that the Serb police and army knew about that. I know about the prison I was in and I know of another prison in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about the prison of the KLA in a basement of the department store in Vucitrn, your place, where Serbs were detained - not only from Vucitrn, but others too - and then were taken to be liquidated? It is a prison that was in the basement, in the cellars of the department store, when KFOR and UNMIK arrived, and that prison was held by the KLA. You were back by then. You would have to have known about that.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true. The storehouse was used by the Serbs to find shelter during the NATO airstrikes. I know that it was used for that purpose and for sheltering the Serb population during the strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say you know nothing about the KLA prison in Vucitrn in the basement of the department store; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that there was a gaol there, no. I say it in full responsibility. There was no prison there, because the cellar of the department store, I said it even in my testimony, that it was used for the needs of the Serb police and army to shelter also civilians, Serb civilians. They sheltered them on the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about another case that took place on Bajram, before the NATO aggression, on the Bajram holiday, when masked members of the KLA in Vucitrn, in front of the family, seized Behmi Muljanu [phoen] - Fehmi Muljanu [phoen] is the name. He was an employee of the republican administration of public income in Vucitrn - only for the sole fact that he didn't want to leave his workplace? Do you know about that? His daughter succeeded in pulling down the mask of one of the KLA members and she recognised a man called Delija, but Uljan Muljanu [phoen] was never found. All he found was his head, which had been cut off, a cut-off head. Do you know about that Albanian in Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fehmi Muljani, there's no such name in Vushtrri. There's no Muljani. I've never heard this surname. I know perfectly well that there were no people of this name. Milosevic, you have erroneous information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... or Muljanu. It makes no difference. One or the other, Munjaku or Munjanu. It might just be a one-letter difference. We can ascertain that.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Fehmi Munjani does not exist. Obtain better information, because you've got false information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say Munjani. I don't know what interpretation you got. A "u," not an "i." Not Munjani, but Munjanku perhaps, an employee of the incomes department who was killed in this way. Say he doesn't exist. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never heard of this surname, Munjani.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I say Fehmi Munjaku, an employee of the republican administration for incomes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are not getting anywhere with this. We're not getting anywhere. Mr. Milosevic, in due course you can present your evidence on the point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. He says he doesn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when, in mid-1998, in the village of Dervare, at Cicavica, a forester by the name of Milan Zivic [phoen] was killed in his own home, in his house?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this case. I was chairman of the Human Rights Council at this time, and I recorded this case and sent it to the Human Rights Council headquarters for consideration. Milan Zivic was killed solely because he had good relations with his Albanian neighbours, and he was killed by Serbs who were angry with him because of these good relations he had with Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not a single one suffered because of that. Milan Zivic was killed by terrorists, and you know that full well. You know that very well.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true. Milan Zivic, I knew him myself. He was a poor man and he always received help from the Albanians and he moved freely wherever he went. The Albanians rather liked him, and this is why somebody killed him. You might know better who killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The terrorists killed Albanians too who were on good relations with the Serbs, not Serbs alone, and you know that full well. Now, do you know the following: That a reserve policeman by the name of Momcili Zivic, from Samodreza, was killed in the yard of his own house?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard this for the first time today. He might have been killed somewhere else and then this might have been used as an alibi. This is the first time I've heard anybody being killed in Samadrexha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps that reserve policeman was killed by Serbs as well. What do you think? What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to make any claims about who killed him, but I don't know who killed him. This is the first time I've heard of this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know when, as soon as KFOR arrived, an active policeman Srdjan Stojkovic from Prelluzhe, was kidnapped on the bridge at Ibar which joins the two parts of Mitrovica? He was taken into the southern part of town and disappeared. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because immediately after NATO arrived, I wasn't in Kosova. And I belong to Vushtrri and not to Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know of another case? How far is Vushtrri in Vucitrn? Not to waste time on that. In the village of Pantina, on June 1998, an eight-member family by the name of Miljkovic was kidnapped, the parents and six children, in the village of Pantina. In June 1998, an eight-member family. The name was Miljkovic; the parents and six children. You know or you don't know. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was something but that it is not true that a family was killed. Somebody -- some member of a Serbian family in Pantina indeed did fire from his own cellar and wounded two Albanians during the night. One of these wounded people is still with us, but what happened next, I don't know, because your police didn't allow us to obtain information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, you're well acquainted with the event that took place in Pantina. What is true that all eight members of the family were kidnapped. Just the mother and father were killed. The children were later released. Do you know about another incident --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: First you say they were all killed and then you say they were all released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will get on more quickly if you don't argue, Mr. Kadriu. Now, Mr. Milosevic, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about Milorad Milic from Prelluzhe, at the end of 1998, when they hit him with a sniper from the Cicavica area which is a KLA bunker was later found? Do you know about that? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1997, no Albanian has been able to visit the village of Prelluzhe. The road has been entirely blocked, and it is still forbidden for Albanians to go through this village. However, the people -- you took the people who were killed in battle --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You don't know. Not to lose time. And even they are -- refused to allow you to commit those atrocities against the Serbs. You have a piece of information -- the next piece of information. The village of Mijalic, Mijalic under Mount Cicavica, two Mitrovic brothers, Ljubisa and Radivoje, are killed. And on the same day, while he was walking along the railroad, the brother of one of these, Miljan Mitrovic, a soldier who had come home on leave. After two months of torture, he managed to escape the KLA prison in Cicavica, this son. But his father and uncle were killed. Do you know about that event?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is that one morning the OSCE found out that a soldier of the Yugoslav army had deserted the army with the aim of going to the area controlled by the KLA where he had his family. This family lived in the area controlled by the KLA and had never had any problems. However, how the murder happened that day when this -- this soldier had deserted and wanted to join his family, you will know this better than me, because until that day, this family had never had problems. And the OSCE knew about this and knew that the family lived in KLA-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's where you helped -- where you killed Ljubisa and Radivoje, both brothers, right there in the Mijalic village, KLA-controlled. Do you know about Velika Vucetic, 65 years old, a woman from Toradza, not far from your own village. She was kidnapped, raped, and she died through burning. Together with her was her daughter Milica. She was burnt too. Do you know about that event?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've heard of this. And in which place did this happen? Could you make this clearer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Toradza, not far from your own village.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard of this case. I've never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You never heard about it. All right. Did you hear --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard about another case, that of an Albanian, Zejnil Munaku -- Zejnil Bunjaku from Vucitrn? That the KLA in Vucitrn, immediately after KFOR's arrival, lynched him in front of a mass of Albanians who had collected there in front of the Kosejda cafe. They killed him because his wife was in fact a Serb. Do you know about that incident?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is ridiculous, Your Honours. I knew Zejnil Bunjaku, and he's still alive and he works in Prishtina for UNMIK. He is still alive and living and working in Prishtina. He travels every day. Your information is wrong, Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I haven't rebuked you before, but don't address the accused in that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can give you -- bring you Zejnil Bunjaku here alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you can bring a Zejnil Bunjaku, probably, I'm sure, but not the one you killed. Do you remember when two brothers died, Zoran and Dejan Milic, in April 1999, by the village of Gojbulja?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Gojbulja is mainly Serbian. And I don't know who died. Deaths do happen. And even today it's still a Serbian village. And people still die. I don't know who died there. This village is not far from Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were killed by a KLA bomb. They didn't die of natural causes. They were killed as a result of a KLA bomb.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could the KLA throw a bomb into the village of Gojbulja when the entire village is Serbian inhabited and the police and the army control the entire area? This is a frame-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And as everything has been made up relating to the times you're talking about, do you know -- and don't just say you were young at the time, I'm asking you whether you know about this next fact, that is to say, the demonstrations that took place in 1968 in Pristina and other towns in Kosovo and Metohija under the Albanian flag, and the tank brigade arrived from Skopje to Pristina in 1968, do you know about the demonstrators, when they went back to their demonstrations that they pledged to kill a Serb? And according to the oath they took after the demonstrations, Bora Djordjevic was killed from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have already dealt with the history of this thing. We're not going back now to 1968. As far as this evidence is concerned, the relevant evidence was the evidence which he gave before us. So I suggest to you, use your remaining time to ask questions about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after KFOR arrived, your representatives attacked the church in Vucitrn and that KFOR had to protect the church? They did not fully destroy it, but they did in Mijalic, Velika Reka, Vrnica, Banjska, and in the village of Samodreza, that is the historic church of Samodreza. Do you know of all these incidents, all of this after the arrival of KFOR. The church in Vucitrn they managed to protect, the KFOR, but in the villages Mijalic, Velika Reka, Vrnica, Banjska, and Samodreza, the historic church of Samodreza, that is, where the Serb army took holy communion before the Battle of Kosovo, all of those churches were destroyed. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The church in Samadrexha, which is indeed an historic church, and it has a role in Albanian history because we haven't always been Muslims, still exists today in Samadrexha. If you wish, send someone to visit it. It exists. It may be slightly damaged, but the church is there, and it has its roof and walls. So I'm telling you that you are receiving false information. As for Vernica, there has never been a church there, because I come from nearby that village. The Court can look at a map to see where the churches are and see whether there was a church in Vernica or not. I'm sure that there was no church there. But there is a church in Samadrexha, and there is a church in Vushtrri, and KFOR is installed in the churchyard in Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise in that church in Samodreza, the one that was destroyed, there are only remains of walls and that is where a garbage dump is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, he's given his answer on this, and you've heard what he said, that the church is still there and there is not one in the other village. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, you do remember that in this village of Samodreza, Ferhat Mujo killed; Danilo Milincic, a young father of two children. I hope you remember that.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in 1981. And if the Court requires it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Out of 45 villages in the municipality of Vucitrn, ethnically Serb or mixed villages where Serbs lived until KFOR arrived, Serbs remain only in six villages now, and in the remaining 39 villages where there are no Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. more Serbs left, Serb houses were either torched or destroyed or taken over by others. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true, because it's not true that there were Serbs in all these villages. There are still Serbs in Prelluzhe, Gojbula, and Grace, but if it did happen in some places that the house of a Serb were burned, it is well known that these are people who committed crimes against the Albanian population, who killed someone, who committed a massacre. So this may have been done in revenge. If somebody had killed members of your family, you would not sit with your arms akimbo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I told you, Mr. Kadriu, not to address the accused in that way during the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said that Serbs remain only in six villages. Of course in Prelluzhe, Grace, Gojbulja, Mijalic, Banjska and -- but I spoke about 39 villages where there are no Serbs left. As for Vucitrn, where you are vice-president of the municipality, there is not a single Serb left. Is that correct or not? Is there a Serb in Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment, there is not. In the town, there is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you cleansed the entire town of Serbs. There's not a single Serb left.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We haven't cleansed it. We haven't cleansed it. They went themselves after they committed crimes against their fellow citizens and dug all those mass graves, all those acts of arson. They went before -- themselves before KFOR came. We didn't send them away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where did they go to?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can say this with the greatest sense of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, where did they go to, the Serbs who left Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the KFOR troops entered, the entire Serbian population that could bear arms was under arms, and so they left the villages of Prelluzhe, Gojbula, and Grace and went to Serbia and went themselves before KFOR entered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is not necessary to use up more time for this. You've said there is not a single Serb left in Vucitrn. That is correct, and that cannot be contested. You talked a lot about refugees here. Do you know about this big gathering of refugees that was mentioned here in the village of Resnik, underneath Cicavica, where allegedly there were 50.000 refugees, and in February 1999, they were visited by Sadako Ogata, tens of thousands? And when she left, all of them went to their own homes. And the next day when people from the municipality of Vucitrn came, there was no one left there except for three young men in this field who said that the KLA organised this gathering so that they could introduce these people as refugees. There was no one left the next day. This was carried by the mass media at that time, after this visit. She had been fooled. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true that this happened in 1999. This happened in 1998 when the Albanians were evicted from their houses, fleeing from the artillery and from the Serbian police and military forces and went to Reznik. And then there they were saved by Sadako Ogata, because if she had not come, that would have become a St. Bartholomew's Eve massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Your concepts as to what would happen or would not have happened are pointless. I don't think we should waste time with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking whether now at 1.00 we do finish or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, you want to examine. Do you want to ask the witness about discrepancies between an earlier statement and his present evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, but this relates to very important things that the witness said a while ago and did not say now. These are only essential questions related to the indictment, nothing else, and also in relation to what the witness said here. There are a few points of capital importance indeed, and I don't think that the Trial Chamber would be able to view problems related to this testimony if not hearing this, so I will really make every effort to speed things up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll certainly hear questions about that, and no doubt we can have some copies of the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I was just going to say, if my friend wants to focus on those, perhaps if the Court had copies of the original statement, the Court can note the discrepancies themselves without taking up further time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if we have copies of the statement, we'll then allow you to cross-examine, if we go on until 1.20, but we'll give Mr. Milosevic another five minutes if he wants it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I want you to abide by the time that you promised yesterday. It was 1.00. Please, yesterday you said that you would finish by 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We never said that. That was a much earlier timetable. Now, do you want to ask the witness anything more?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't want to extend this sitting around here, because practically you've shortened my time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tapuskovic, the quickest way to deal with this is if you would take us to the page where the point you want to make is and we can deal then briefly with it with the witness. But we can follow along with you where you say there are points to be made, and we'll try and deal with this as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall make every effort, but before me I have the Serb version. It coincides with the English version. What I'm going to start with skips the first page, and this, what I'm referring to, is on the second page. May I start with my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please just give yes or no answers so that we could do what we're supposed to do in the next 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During your testimony, you said that the secret police brought you into custody several times and that they did certain unpleasant things.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The police -- the MUP took us into custody. Please let me give the explanation. I want to explain to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, we are under pressure of time, and therefore please keep the answers short. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that many secret student groups were established.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no secret student groups. There were -- we were students that were prosecuted by the secret police only because of wanting Kosova to become a republic, and some of us went to gaol for 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were verbal sentences, absurd ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you join the movement for the freedom of the Albanian region? Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was a student, I was a member of the illegal movement demanding Kosova to become a republic, but our activity was only through demonstration. That was the way we expressed our discontent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did this movement operate in Kosovo, Macedonia, and everywhere else where Albanians lived?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this movement operated in Kosova. That is what I know. This was a student movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was its primary objective to have an Albania in which the entire Albanian people would live?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our aim then was to advance the status of Kosova from a region into a republic in the context of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to point out one thing to you. You told the investigator that this movement operated in Kosovo and in Macedonia and everywhere else where Albanians lived, and that in addition to that, in addition to Kosova becoming a republic, your objective was to have an Albania where the entire Albanian people would live. That is what you stated on the 2nd of December, 2000. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That does not mean that there weren't other organisations that had such aspirations, but I'm talking here about the student organisation where I was a member. I cannot rule out the possibility for the existence of such organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. You said that that was your dream.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are wrong. Our dream would be to unite Kosova with Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is sufficient for me. Could you tell me: Drenica, as a geographical term, does it include one quarter of Kosovo, or how much, in your estimate?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the size in kilometres. It is a region situated in the centre of Kosova. I don't have any idea in terms of kilometres how big that is. I don't know how big that is. I was never interested to find that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If it's not one quarter of Kosovo, how big could it be? Could you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, I don't know how big that region is. I may give you the names of towns that are found in that region, but I can't give you numbers or sizes. I can't do that. I can't speak in kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know what happened on the 28th of February, in the morning, on the 28th of February, 1998? You know what happened then? What did happen then on the 28th of February, 1998?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of February, 1998, I am repeating here for the umpteenth time that Serb police and army attacked the villages of Cirez and Likovc [phoen], and they killed many people, many civilians there. Likoshan, sorry. All were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that day, in your house, you heard artillery fire in your own house? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, more than correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You encountered some people after that, and they told you that Serb forces had rounded the villagers of Likoshan, Cirez, Baks. "According to what they told us, on the previous day there was an exchange of gunfire between the KLA and Serbs, and on that occasion in Cirez two Serb policemen were killed." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I heard these shots, I went up to Dubofc village, which is found in Vushtrri municipality, and from the people who were fleeing the police encirclement, they told me that there people were killed by Serb forces, someone, but they didn't know who that was. They didn't know what really happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. But the Serb forces came to that village only on the next day, after two policemen had been killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I am repeating. I didn't know who got killed. I just got the news from the people who were fleeing the scene, who had left their own homes and were heading towards Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I said to you is what you said to the investigators on the 2nd of December, 2000. What I just said to you now, that is what you said then, the way you had heard it read by me.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't see the point here. I do not deny that I didn't know who was killed, whether I found out that ten members were killed from Ahmeti family and some others from Sejdia family, but then I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we may be able to make better progress if you simply read out the parts of the statement to the witness, those on which you want to rely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I'd like to read to the witness. He said the following on that occasion: "I first heard of the KLA in 1991." That's what he said here. "But only in 1997 they were in a position to organise themselves sufficiently and start guerrilla attacks against the Serb army and police.
