However, only in 1998 the KLA really became a true force, because they managed to take the area, the entire area, that of Drenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, that the entire area of Drenica was taken by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am repeating what I already said. On the 28th of November, 1997, the Kosovo Liberation Army became a public phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the passage, Mr. Tapuskovic. It may be sensible to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now, why am I asking this? On page 7, in the first, second, third, fourth, fifth paragraph, you said to the investigators: "Earlier on, the war between the Serbs and the KLA broke out in Drenica in 1998. I think it was sometime around the month of June. I had to register all the refugees who came to Vucitrn, from the area of Drenica. The municipalities of Vucitrn and Mitrovica, there was a flood of refugees that was coming in. I think that from the war zone, about 40.000 refugees came." And this was in 1998. That is not what was happening in 1999, when people set out to Macedonia and Albania, but in 1998. From that area, where there were skirmishes between the KLA and the army, 40.000 refugees fled from that area, and you registered them and you received them in Vucitrn, where there was peace. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that during June, July 1998, the Albanian population of these areas had become prey to artillery fire by the Serb army and police. Therefore, they were obliged, because of this fighting - because now even the KLA had entered into the war with the Serb forces - because of the fighting, the population had started to leave in the face of the violence that was being exercised by the Serb forces that entered from one house to another. They came and found shelter in three municipalities: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prishtina, Vushtrri, and Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier, you said that because of this war between the KLA and the army and the police, that the population fled and came to Vucitrn. That is what you said in your witness statement earlier on.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you have taken the statement. The truth is that the population were forced to leave and to flee their homes and settle in these three municipalities. Because numerous forces, with tanks, armoured cars, had encircled the villages; therefore, they had to flee and settle in the above-mentioned communes: Prishtina, Vushtrri, and Mitrovica [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said earlier on that the period between 1998 until February 1999 was relatively peaceful, however, that there were clashes between the Serbs and the KLA; is that correct, in that period as well?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. There was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then the bombing started. And now we are coming to the 1st of April, when, together with your family, you set out. You said what you did with your family. They boarded a bus, but you went to Gornja Studime with your friends. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. I did not board the bus at all. My family did. Then they got down again, because the bus was overcrowded with people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I said: Your family boarded a bus.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't need to take a bus to Studime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You went to Gornja Studime?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day I went through Studime e Eperme and settled in between Veseli and Sesekov village, at a friend of mine's house who is a professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge May, could he just answer me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said earlier on that you went to Gornja Studime in order to spend the night there in the house of Musa Terbunja, who was commander of the KLA for that area. "This area was under KLA control and then we went to Cecile, where the KLA had some kind of headquarters." Is that correct, what you said a while ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where is -- just a moment. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 12, page 13. Now I'm going to move on to page 13. This is the end of page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's in the middle of page 13 in the English, which is a different type set out.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Studime village I went. It was the 2nd of April when I went there. There I only passed. I was there in passing. I rested a while. There was no staff of KLA there in Studime e Eperme. From there I went to another village, Vesekovc, in a neighbourhood between the two villages that I mentioned, at a friend of mine, a professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge May, I have so little time left. Please, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. What your statement says, Mr. Kadriu, is that you stayed at the house of Musa Terbunja, who was the KLA commander of the area. Did you stay with the KLA commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that night. How could the KLA commander come to that house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said no. I stayed there for a while and then I went on my way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us how it is that your statement apparently includes the statement that you stayed with the KLA commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The KLA commander was not then -- he was not in Studime e Eperme. I met him, as I did many other people, on the way, and then I continued my way. I had to go somewhere else to pass the night, whereas that commander was one of the people I met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, perhaps another passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm moving on to the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "I remained there for the following month," not two days. "I stayed there for another month. The houses in Cecelija were full of refugees from different places, because this area was considered to be safe, as it was under KLA control." And the last sentence there: "I don't know the exact number, but I think that in different small villages in this area under the control of the KLA, there were over 30.000 refugees." Is that the way you described it then?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Over 30.000 refugees were there, and I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to omit the next paragraph, but I'll come back to it. And then what follows is the following. You're putting it this way: The KLA resisted the Serbs there where they were protecting these refugees. How did they do that? That's what I'm asking you. First of all, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: For some months on end, the KLA tried not to let the Serb forces penetrate where the civilian population was housed. That is a fact. But they were unable, because of shortages of munitions, to do that, so they said, "We are unable to protect the civilian population who are there; therefore, they need to find a solution."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's what you explained last time as well. Now, before I move on, I would like to go back to this other paragraph here on that same page. Yesterday, here in Court, you said that you saw those two MiGs above Popovo. Can you explain this in greater detail? How did you see those two MiGs?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're wrong, either the translation is wrong. I didn't say I saw the MiGs. I only heard the detonation. In Popova, Sahit Surdulli had seen the MiGs. He's an economist. He stayed as a refugee in Popova, and he had seen those MiG planes with his own eyes throwing the bombs over this village, as they did in Bajgora village too. I didn't see them with my own eyes. I was in Samadrexha and Cecelia then, in that place between these two villages. I heard the noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I must have stated in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But on the 2nd of May, which means when you were in another place, with Sllakofc with your friend, Fadil Beqiri: "I went there because Fadil's nephew, Faruk Beqiri, a KLA soldier, was to be buried there," although you said you went to attend the funeral of a woman who died at the front line - and that's why I'm asking you - from Serb fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your point will be lost on us if you don't tell us what page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps I can in English. It's page 14, Judge, in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the Serbian version in my hands. That's the problem. The witness said yesterday that he attended the funeral of a woman, but he says here that he attended the funeral of the nephew, et cetera, who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can read that. We can read that. Why don't you go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested is was how far that front line was from the place you were at to attend the funeral. How far was the front line from you and from the rest of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb army had captured some positions in Bajgora Mountains and had come closer to the villages where we were, but at about 12.00 the burial ceremony took place. The nephew of Fadil was buried there. At the same time, the refugees who were settled in villages in which the Serb army had started to deploy had begun to evacuate from those villages, so while the burial ceremony was going on, they kept moving away from these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, you arrived in Cecile - and you went because you had to go - and when you arrived in Cecile, there were KLA soldiers there, too. And that's the next paragraph. There were KLA soldiers there, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some soldiers who were leaving at that moment. I saw them leaving. On the opposite side, the population took to the Shala hills and mountains, on the opposite of the column. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you said that you had the possibility of going with members of the KLA, but you took to the hills; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did have the chance of going in the opposite direction, but I didn't because I was with people with whom I had shared all my problems in the past month, and it would not have been good for me, as chairman of the human rights council, to abandon these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you went to the top of the hill, by Cecilia, is that right? You went to the top of the hill and went further on?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire column went in that direction, to the top of the hill. And when we arrived there, Serbian forces started machine-gun fire from the village of Skocna, at the convoy. There, there were two KLA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But that's not what you said. You said that you came across soldiers there, three KLA soldiers, in fact, who told you to go to Gornja Studime and to take a different route. They instructed you. They sent you there. That's what you said before.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They merely guided the column to go away from the point where they could be seen by Serbian forces, because Serbian forces were firing at the column. And they told them to change their route so they wouldn't be seen by Serbian forces, and they didn't continue that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, can you wind up in five minutes, please, because we have already gone five minutes over the 20 past. So just find the main points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the main points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So this convoy of 30.000 people went on, and while it was going onwards, you didn't mention that anybody shot at you, but some people arrived and told us that by the transformer station nearby Gornja Sebenia [phoen], that some people were killed by Serb fire. That's what you said. You didn't say that anybody actually shot at the column there.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian forces continually fired on the convoy from Skocna and so those two KLA soldiers were positioned there to point people into a -- in a direction away from the one where they could be seen. When we arrived at Studime e Eperme, a girl was hit from firing from the hills, and we were continually under the fire of Serbian forces. The convoy was so long that you couldn't find out what was happening at the beginning and at the end, but we were always under fire. It was a great crowd of people, 30.000 people on the move.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. To speed things up, what happened was: As you approached the Serb forces, you stuck out a white flag; is that right? You put out a white flag?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't put out the white flag. You must get a better translation. There was somebody else who was carrying the white flag at the head of the column, and I gave them first the name and surname of the person yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that you were carrying it. You went to the head of the column and you learnt there that this white flag was being displayed because you might encounter Serb forces; is that it?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was put in a tub full of gravel. The Serbs were only 300 metres away from the place where the white flag was, and they could see the white flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And it was only then that the Serbs arrived, only after that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. People had started to settle in and to make themselves -- dig themselves in at that area, and meanwhile Cecelia had started to burn. Meanwhile, Serbian forces had started to arrive at 2100 hours. I explained that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I won't insist on that. But it was from there that the Serb forces took you to the prison in the gymnasium, in the gym hall. Up until then, the Serbs hadn't arrived then, were they? They arrived at that moment.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we were surrounded by Serbian forces on all sides. And also Serbian civilians from Prelluzhe, not just from military forces and police forces. The entire convoy was surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, but up until then, there were no Serbs. Who was with you until that time? The KLA.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The convoy -- the KLA, between Samadrexha, and Studime e Eperme, had the two last soldiers that you can see on the video, and nobody else arrived at the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted to say. You said that there were no KLA soldiers, whereas they escorted you up to that spot, and on the film that you brought, you could see the members of the KLA approaching you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The two KLA members you can see on the video, they were in the place between Studime e Eperme and Cecelia village. After that, they left. They didn't come with us. They told the column of people to change course because they didn't want to be hit by the snipers who were -- kept firing at us. The column kept moving. We were perhaps the last in the row.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two more questions, with the Court's indulgence, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First, when you went to prison, you were questioned there to see whether you were perhaps a member of the KLA, because -- but once it was clarified that you weren't a suspect, you were released and you went off in the direction you left in; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just answer very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were accused of terrorism. We were all released with the exception of one whose fate I don't know. All of us, young and old, were accused of terrorism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now I should like to read out something else you said when you were at the border itself, when you were at the very border, and that is paragraph 3, page 19. You say: "We ran along the main road. On one side were the Serb bunkers. We were lucky because NATO planes were flying over the area and bombing it so that the Serbs didn't touch us." That's what you said at the time. Is that true, because of NATO's bombing that was taking place, that you fared as you did?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 20, English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even yesterday I wanted to explain it, but because of the time restraint, I didn't. On the way from Prizren to -- from Shtime to the border, we were escorted by Serb paramilitaries who used us as cannon fodder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. At the border, when you were at the border itself, because of NATO bombing which you confirm here --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- you went on your way and that the Serbs didn't touch you because of that.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs, while we were walking from Zhur village to the customs point, some Serbs tried to waylay us. They were soldiers in uniforms. They tried to do that, but the NATO aeroplanes moved constantly, were flying constantly. I think that was the reason for our salvation. Otherwise, we would have been looted or something else would have happened to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, but I would have a lot more assistance to give to the Trial Chamber if the circumstances were different, but if you say so, very well. I'll end there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will exhibit this document which will be -- if we can have a number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tapuskovic, if there are other passages which you wish to draw our attention to, then hand in a document suitably marked and we will take it into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That was one of the things I wanted to make sure, is that that got an exhibit number. Second thing is I will forego any re-examination. I had a number of issues. Time constraints, I won't do it. However, in fairness to the accused and the Court, we did indicate yesterday that we would have a further meeting concerning witnesses. I will now propose to hand out, perhaps even after we adjourn, to the various parties the new witness list, and I think I should advise the Court that it is our plan for Monday morning to start with Mr. Sakir Tac, and Mr. Saxon, who has joined us in the courtroom today, with the Court's permission, will be leading that witness on Monday, followed by Mr. Loku who has been moved up on the list. So that is the immediate change. The rest will be self-evident. I think those are the issues that I wanted to raise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will adjourn now until half past nine on Monday. Mr. Kadriu, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour
